name: The Thucydides Trap
statement: When a rising power threatens to displace a ruling one, the resulting fear makes war dangerously likely.
statementAccent: the resulting fear makes war dangerously likely
meaning: The Thucydides Trap refers to the apparent structural tendency toward war when a rising power threatens to displace an existing ruling power. It names the dangerous stress that arises when a rapidly rising power rivals an established one: the rising power's growing strength and assertiveness collide with the ruling power's fear, insecurity, and determination to defend its position, generating a dynamic that makes violent conflict likely, though, as its author repeatedly stresses, not inevitable. The mechanism is driven by two forces Thucydides identified in the ancient case, the rise of the challenger and the fear it instils in the incumbent.
mechanism: The trap works through the interaction of rising confidence and settled fear. As the challenger grows, it demands more say, more respect, and more room, while the incumbent, alarmed, hardens its stance to preserve its rank. Each side's prudent response feeds the other's alarm, and third-party crises can drag both into a war neither sought. Graham Allison anchored this in a line from Thucydides, that it was the rise of Athens and the fear this instilled in Sparta that made war inevitable, and his research team examined sixteen historical cases over some five hundred years, finding that twelve of them ended in war.

examples.text: The archetype, from Thucydides' history of the Peloponnesian War, in which Athens's rise and the fear it stirred in Sparta drove the two into a ruinous conflict.
Allison's project identified sixteen cases in five centuries where a rising power threatened a ruling one, and found twelve ended in war, the source of the often-quoted three-in-four figure.
Allison's central contemporary application, framing a rising China challenging the ruling United States, and asking whether the two can escape the trap.

variants.name: The four escapes
variants.text: The four of sixteen cases that avoided war, which Allison credits to imaginative statecraft, the basis for his claim that war is likely but not inevitable.

variants.name: Earlier uses of the phrase
variants.text: The novelist Herman Wouk used 'Thucydides's trap' as early as 1980 for the US-Soviet rivalry, so Allison revived and popularised the term rather than coining it.

whyItMatters: The concept became one of the most influential shorthands in contemporary great-power politics, giving policymakers, journalists, and scholars a vivid vocabulary for framing US-China strategic competition and the structural risks of a power transition. It has been invoked in high-level policy debate, features in international-relations curricula, and functions as a reference point in arguments about whether great-power war is avoidable and what statecraft is required to avoid it. Its influence rests as much on its rhetorical power and historical resonance as on its contested empirical claims.

working.text: read the risk of great-power war as the interaction of a challenger's rise and an incumbent's fear, not either alone.
use the trap as a warning that demands deliberate statecraft, since a minority of historical cases avoided war.
cite the sixteen-cases, twelve-wars tally as Allison's claim, not an established law, given the disputes over its method.

limits: The concept is heavily contested by historians and international-relations scholars. Critics argue the choice of which sixteen rivalries to include is not derived from a rigorous, replicable rule, so the twelve-in-sixteen ratio is an artefact of selection, and the coding of cases as war or no war, and of who is rising, is often ambiguous. It is faulted as mono-causal and structurally deterministic, foregrounding a single variable while downplaying domestic politics, leadership choices, and contingency, and as misreading Thucydides, whose account of the Peloponnesian War's causes is far more multi-causal. And correlation is not causation: even granting the tally, co-occurrence does not establish that the transition caused the wars.
misreadings: Allison does not say US-China war is inevitable; he argues it is likely absent deliberate effort but escapable, and avoidance is his whole prescriptive point. The sixteen-cases, twelve-wars finding is not settled empirical fact but a disputed methodology, its figures accurately reported yet its case selection and coding contested. Thucydides did not describe a trap; he wrote the underlying sentence about Athens and Sparta, and the trap framing and the generalisation across five centuries are Allison's. And Allison popularised rather than coined the phrase.
origin: Coined in its modern usage by the political scientist Graham Allison, first in a 2012 Financial Times article and developed in a 2015 Atlantic piece and the 2017 book 'Destined for War', named for the ancient Greek historian Thucydides; the phrase had earlier been used by Herman Wouk in 1980.

sources.text: Allison, 'The Thucydides Trap: Are the U.S. and China Headed for War?,' The Atlantic (2015). — the concept and the US-China application.
Thucydides's Trap Case File, Harvard Belfer Center. — the sixteen cases and twelve wars.
